title: GIS-Based Flood Risk Mapping
subtitle: Remote sensing + ML for flood vulnerability analysis
description: An automated pipeline that ingests satellite imagery and DEM data to produce flood risk maps using terrain analysis and machine learning classification. Integrated with QGIS for visualization and field validation workflows.

evolution.title: Initial Concept
evolution.description: Identified the need for automated flood risk assessment after studying manual surveying limitations.

evolution.title: Research & Planning
evolution.description: Reviewed literature on remote sensing-based flood mapping. Defined dataset requirements and processing pipeline architecture.

evolution.title: Pipeline Development
evolution.description: Building the satellite data ingestion, DEM processing, and ML classification modules. Currently integrating Google Earth Engine API.

evolution.title: QGIS Plugin & Web Dashboard
evolution.description: Package as a QGIS plugin and build a lightweight web dashboard for non-GIS users.

evolution.title: Real-time SAR Integration
evolution.description: Integrate Sentinel-1 SAR data for near-real-time flood detection during active events.

problemsFaced: Google Earth Engine API rate limits causing processing delays
Inconsistent DEM resolution across study area
Cloud cover in optical imagery — 60% of Sentinel-2 images unusable
failedAttempts: Tried using Landsat 8 initially — spatial resolution too coarse for urban flood mapping
First ML model (Random Forest) overfit on training tiles with zero flood events
SRTM DEM had artefacts over water bodies that corrupted terrain analysis
lessonsLearned: SAR data is far superior to optical for active flood mapping — it penetrates clouds
Stratified sampling for train/test split is essential when classes are heavily imbalanced
Always validate DEM data quality before running terrain derivatives
futureWork: Expand to river basin scale with hydrological routing
Add uncertainty quantification to ML predictions
Explore transfer learning from flood events in other geographies
journal.notes: This project is teaching me more about data quality than about ML. The engineering fundamentals matter more than the algorithm choice.

buildAnalytics.breakdown: AI used for boilerplate data processing code and literature review summarization. Core algorithm design, GIS methodology, and validation are manual.

title: Structural Load Optimizer
subtitle: Python-based beam and slab load distribution tool
description: A command-line and web tool that takes structural geometry as input and computes load paths, bending moments, and shear force diagrams for simple beam and slab configurations. Designed as a learning tool for structural analysis.

evolution.title: Course Assignment Origin
evolution.description: Started as a structural analysis assignment. Decided to build a reusable tool instead of solving it once on paper.

evolution.title: Scope Definition
evolution.description: Limited to simply supported beams and one-way slabs. Defined input format and output visualizations.

evolution.title: Core Engine
evolution.description: Implemented stiffness matrix methods and Matplotlib-based SFD/BMD plotting.

evolution.title: Streamlit Web App
evolution.description: Wrapped in Streamlit for interactive use by classmates and faculty.

evolution.title: 2D Frame Analysis
evolution.description: Extend to full 2D frame analysis with multiple load cases and IS 456 code checks.

problemsFaced: Numerical instability in stiffness matrix inversion for near-zero element lengths
Streamlit session state management was confusing initially
failedAttempts: First tried using symbolic math (SymPy) — too slow for real-time updates
lessonsLearned: Numerical methods need careful handling of boundary conditions
Streamlit is powerful for quick engineering dashboards but has real limitations for complex state
journal.notes: First project where I felt the connection between theory and code. The moment diagrams matching textbook answers felt genuinely satisfying.

buildAnalytics.breakdown: Almost entirely manual. AI only used to generate docstrings.

title: ArchiOS
subtitle: Digital Engineering Operating System
description: This platform itself — a full-stack Next.js application that serves as my digital headquarters. Documents projects, engineering journals, knowledge graphs, and manages a dual civil + data science identity.

evolution.title: Frustration with conventional portfolios
evolution.description: Every portfolio looked the same. Wanted something that shows how I think, not just what I finished.

evolution.title: OS Concept & Architecture
evolution.description: Designed the Digital Engineering OS concept. Mapped all features: dual identity, project DNA, knowledge graph, engineering journal, AI lab.

evolution.title: Core Platform Build
evolution.description: Building the full Next.js application with all modules.

evolution.title: Vercel Deployment + Domain
evolution.description: Deploy to Vercel, connect custom domain, configure GitHub integration webhook.

evolution.title: AI Avatar + Voice Assistant
evolution.description: Add conversational AI layer that can answer questions about my projects and background.

problemsFaced: Balancing civil engineering and data science identities in a single coherent UI
Knowledge graph performance with many nodes — D3 force simulation gets expensive
failedAttempts: First draft was just a dark-themed conventional portfolio — scrapped it entirely
Tried Three.js for knowledge graph — too heavy for the use case
lessonsLearned: Design philosophy matters as much as technical implementation
D3 force simulation needs careful parameter tuning for stable, readable graphs
futureWork: AI recommendation engine for project connections
journal.notes: Building the tool you use is the most honest form of dogfooding.

buildAnalytics.breakdown: AI assisted heavily with component scaffolding and styling. Architecture design, feature conception, and data modeling are entirely manual.
